# Part VII: Evaluation {#part-evaluation .unnumbered}

> "All models are wrong, but some are useful."
>
> George E. P. Box, ["All models are wrong"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_models_are_wrong)

Evaluation results feed back into every training run, product gate, safety
rule, and model choice. A single number changes what teams optimize. The choice
of judge shapes which behavior post-training rewards, and an agent benchmark
shapes the harness as much as the model. Evaluation is therefore part of the
system it measures.

@sec-benchmarks starts with the conditions a benchmark number depends on:
held-out data that no training stage has seen, a clean harness, stable scoring,
and the ways each condition degrades over time. From there,
@sec-statistical-reliability asks whether the observed difference is large
enough to believe. @sec-human-evaluation-rubrics treats the human label as the
output of a designed measurement instrument, whose rubric and rating protocol
determine what the label means. @sec-judging-holistic moves to model judges and
preference rankings, where the grader has its own biases and may itself be one
of the systems being ranked. @sec-factuality-grounding separates fluency from
support by decomposing answers into claims and evidence, and
@sec-evaluating-agents adds state, tools, and consequences: grading an agent
means inspecting the state of the environment after the task, in addition to the
agent's own report of what it did. @sec-operational-evaluation ends the part by
asking which measurements should block a release, trigger a rollback, or become
the next regression case.

Taken together, the chapters give criteria for telling which numbers deserve
to move a decision, which should only open an investigation, and which mostly
measure the harness that produced them.
